newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN polls employees on 25 varieties of harassment.
newsitem.headline: UN polls employees on 25 varieties of harassment.

text.p: Often accused of ignoring or mishandling sexual harassment, the United Nations is asking its huge staff about sexual, religious, cultural, racial, age, national, racial and many other types of harrassment or abuse.

The 13-page questionnaire, obtained by Reuters, will be the largest survey of its kind in the United Nations and perhaps the world, where officials hope it will eventually reach more than 50,000 staff around the world. New York-based staff was expected to receive the survey shortly.

In addition to sexual harassment, the survey asks about harassment based on race, gender, religion, disability, age, culture, sexual orientation, national origins, language, physical appearance and marital status among others.

It also asks if anyone had been harassed in their personal staff evaluation, in their work load, in getting or not getting promotions, in being assigned overtime and if anyone had experienced verbal or physical abuse.

The questionnaire says a precise definition of harassment was deliberately omitted because of the "unique characteristics" of the United Nations with its swirl of cultures, nationalities and languages.

The downside of being an international civil servant is a lack of protection of national or international law against discrimination. Procedures for whistle-blowing have only been refined in the last few years, and mainly in New York.
"The questionnaire has been designed so that the staff themselves ... will help set both the definitions and the standards for the United Nations work place," the form's introduction says.

The first sexual harassment suit to be settled by the United Nations was in 1995 when American Catherine Claxton was awarded more than $210,000 compensation and costs after what many said was a mishandling of her original complaint.

Another publicised case around the same time was against a protocol official in Geneva, who U.N. sources say was first found guilty of sexual harassment, then cleared of charges, then suspended for other offences and then back on the job.

Over the years the conduct of peacekeeping troops, cobbled together from many countries has been a growing sore. In Cambodia in 1992, complaints about bar fights, brawls, shootouts, brothels, thievery and general drunkenness were legion. Open allegations of abuse by U.N. women employees brought the retort that "boys will be boys."
An investigation into U.N. troops in Bosnia, in the eyes of many, was weak and often whitewashed incidents, although countries were forced to send home offenders more quickly.
